newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia criticised for slashing immigration.
newsitem.headline: Australia criticised for slashing immigration.

text.p: Australian political, business and ethnic groups on Thursday attacked the government's big cut to 1997/98 migrant numbers, which race row politician Pauline Hanson claimed was due to her anti-immigration campaign.
Critics said the cut was economically counter-productive, citing a raft of government and private sector studies that found immigration actually boosted employment.
Victorian state premier Jeff Kennett said the cut would be seen by some people as a response to the increasingly popular Hanson, who has called for an end to immigration.
"I hope that their decision has nothing to do with those elements," Kennett said in a radio interview.

"None of us have any reasons to fear immigration, we need to grow our population, it does create demand and it's very good," he said. "The reduction in immigration is definitely wrong and not in Australia's best interests."
But the leader of the influential Australian Democrats Party said Howard had caved in to Hanson, who opinion polls now rank as potentially the third power in domestic politics.
"John Howard has looked at the polls, as usual, and he has caved in to Pauline Hanson," Cheryl Kernot said.
"It is clear as crystal to me they're running scared and you'll see more of this in the future," Kernot said.
Australia's conservative government on Wednesday announced migrant numbers would be cut by eight percent in the year from July in a move it said would fight chronic unemployment.
Unemployment is currently 8.7 percent and projected to remain high for some time.
But the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said immigration provided an economic and social boost to the country.
"(The chamber) rejects the myth that immigration causes unemployment. There is simply no evidence to support that spurious argument," said chief executive Mark Paterson.
But Hanson, saying the government was spurred into action by her campaign, said high immigration levels in previous years had thrown Australians out of work.
"We have to start looking after our own here first and foremost," Hanson said in a radio interview.
"The unemployment rate in this country, it's far much higher than a lot of other countries throughout the world and yet we still bring in migrants into Australia," she said.
Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock said on Wednesday immigration levels would be cut to 68,000 in the fiscal year from July, down from 74,000 the previous year.
It was the 14-month-old government's second big cut to migrant numbers, after a 13,000 reduction within months of winning office in March 1996.
The approval process has also been revised to favour people with work skills and reduce the number of people joining relatives, a shift likely to hit Asian migrants hardest.
The Ethnic Communities' Council in New South Wales state, Australia's largest, said the cuts boosted Hanson's campaign.

"The changes to the migration programme, on top of cuts to the Human Rights Commission, confirm the worst fears for all Australians who value our multicultural society," said council official Angela Chan.
